title: Ferroelastic exciton splitting in hybrid perovskite nanowalls
authors: Afreen, J. Delgado-Alvarez, H. Krishna Mishra, J. Castillo-Seoane, Koustav Maiti, Pravrati Taank, A. Borras, A. Barranco, Surajit Saha, Priya Mahadevan, J. R. Sanchez-Valencia, K. V. Adarsh
abstract: Hybrid metal-halide perovskites are soft semiconductors in which electronic excitations are strongly influenced by lattice distortions and structural phase transitions. An important open question is whether ferroelastic symmetry breaking merely broadens optical resonances or instead modifies excitonic states through exciton-lattice coupling. Here, we address this question using highly aligned MAPbI3 nanowalls fabricated by glancing-angle deposition, enabling symmetry-selective coupling between ferroelastic texture, structural anisotropy, and a well-defined optical axis. Combining temperature-dependent photoluminescence, X-ray diffraction and polarization-resolved ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy, we observe a polarization-selective excitonic splitting in the orthorhombic phase at 5 K, characterized by orthogonal optical selection rules and a 45 meV energy separation. Near 160 K, where orthorhombic and tetragonal phases coexist, a lower-energy lattice-coupled excitation emerges 58 meV below the centre of the anisotropically split excitonic structure, consistent with coupling between excitonic and lattice-dressed states. At higher temperatures, these excitations progressively acquire lattice-dressed character accompanied by reduced optical anisotropy. A symmetry-guided effective Hamiltonian captures the evolution from anisotropically split excitons to coupled excitonic and lattice-dressed states across the structural transition. Our results show that ferroelastic texture and phase coexistence can modify exciton-lattice coupling, providing a route to symmetry-selective optical responses in soft polar semiconductors.
summary: The research investigates how ferroelastic phase transitions affect excitonic behavior in perovskite nanowalls. By using polarization-resolved ultrafast spectroscopy, the authors observe clear, symmetry-dependent splitting of exciton states that evolves into lattice-coupled excitations across temperature changes. This confirms that structural anisotropy and domain texture provide a powerful mechanism for engineering optical responses in soft polar semiconductors.
main_problem: The study addresses whether ferroelastic symmetry breaking merely causes optical resonance broadening or actively modifies excitonic states through exciton-lattice coupling in soft semiconductors.
main_result: The research demonstrates polarization-selective excitonic splitting and the emergence of lower-energy lattice-coupled excitations, confirming that ferroelastic texture and phase coexistence tune anisotropic exciton-lattice coupling.
method: A combination of advanced experimental techniques including temperature-dependent photoluminescence, X-ray diffraction, and polarization-resolved ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy is employed, complemented by theoretical modeling using an effective Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The system under study is hybrid metal-halide perovskites (MAPbI3) fabricated into highly aligned nanowalls. The physics is modeled using a symmetry-guided effective Hamiltonian that describes the coupling between anisotropic excitonic states and lattice-dressed excitations across structural phase transitions.
key_observables: Polarization-selective excitonic splitting ($\sim 45 	ext{ meV}$), lower-energy lattice-coupled excitation ($58 	ext{ meV}$), optical anisotropy parameter, and temperature dependence of spectral features.
important_parameters: Temperature (especially near $160 	ext{ K}$ transition), energy separation ($\Delta$), and polarization configuration (co-linear vs. cross-linear).
main_assumptions: The use of highly aligned nanowalls is crucial to overcome averaging effects found in disordered films, allowing for symmetry-selective measurements.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the temperature evolution of structural phases and excitonic response, showing polarization-selective splitting in nanowalls compared to planar films; one figure details the GLAD setup and texture analysis.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing a symmetry-selective experimental platform (nanowalls), characterizing the structural transitions via XRD/PFM, measuring the optical dynamics using TA spectroscopy across temperature regimes, and finally modeling the observed evolution using an effective Hamiltonian to explain the coupling mechanism.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses open questions in soft matter quantum optics by linking macroscopic symmetry breaking (ferroelasticity) to microscopic electronic structure modification (excitons), which is highly relevant for designing novel optoelectronic materials.
